excerpt from the sample questionnaire dealing with Richmond illustrates what is meant by "supportive services":
Q. What percent (%) of business services such as banking, attorneys, accountants, doctors, warehouses, advertising, employment services, etc., in the new area come from base municipality?
A. 87.0%.
This response corresponds to our findings concerning the locational alignment of urban area economic activities discussed above and describes one element in the linkage between central city and outlying suburban areas.
Our critique of the Short Haul Committee's presentation of economic data does not mean that we consider it entirely invalid. Doubtless, the economic situation of certain cities does conflict with the general conclusions of the Interim Report. For example, the two largest cities studied by the Committee are San Antonio and Houston, Tex., both of which seem to be in clear contradiction to the trend of "suburban sprawl." It must be pointed out, however, that Texas is among those States having laws which make annexation very easy, and San Antonio and Houston have extended their corporate limits well into the surrounding countryside in anticipation of future settlement and commercial development. The existence of contradictions such as these reflect on the merits of commercial zone expansion by general rule, a subject reserved for discussion at a subsequent stage of this report.
